title: The Lion and the Mouse
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Lion asleep in his lair was waked up by a Mouse running over his face. Losing his temper he seized it with his paw and was about to kill it. The Mouse, terrified, piteously entreated him to spare its life. "Please let me go," it cried, "and one day I will repay you for your kindness." The idea of so insignificant a creature ever being able to do anything for him amused the Lion so much that he laughed aloud, and good-humouredly let it go. But the Mouse's chance came, after all. One day the Lion got entangled in a net which had been spread for game by some hunters, and the Mouse heard and recognised his roars of anger and ran to the spot. Without more ado it set to work to gnaw the ropes with its teeth, and succeeded before long in setting the Lion free. "There!" said the Mouse, "you laughed at me when I promised I would repay you: but now you see, even a Mouse can help a Lion."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what wakes the Lion up at the start?
options: A loud roar from another lion
Hunters approaching his lair
A Mouse running over his face
The sound of a net being spread

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Lion do the moment he wakes?
options: He seizes the Mouse with his paw
He runs out of the lair in fear
He calls out to the hunters
He falls back asleep at once

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Mouse promise the Lion if he is let go?
options: That he will never enter the lair again
That he will bring the Lion some food
That he will warn the Lion about the hunters
That he will repay the Lion's kindness one day

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Lion react to the Mouse's promise?
options: He grows angrier and refuses
He laughs aloud and lets it go
He asks the Mouse to prove it first
He ignores the Mouse and falls asleep

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Lion later get trapped?
options: He falls into a deep pit
He is chased into a river
He gets entangled in a net spread by hunters
He is caught in a storm

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Mouse free the Lion from the net?
options: By gnawing through the ropes with its teeth
By untying the knots with its paws
By calling other mice to help pull the net
By biting through the hunters' spears

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Lion find the Mouse's promise so amusing?
options: He believes the Mouse is joking about the hunters
He does not understand what a promise is
He thinks the Mouse wants to trade places with him
He thinks a creature so small could never truly help him

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Mouse run to the spot when it hears the Lion's roars?
options: It is curious about the sound of hunters
It recognizes the Lion and comes to help him
It is fleeing from a predator of its own
It wants to see the net for itself

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Mouse "piteously entreated" the Lion?
options: It threatened him if he did not comply
It bargained with him over a price
It begged him in a way meant to stir pity
It ignored him and tried to run away

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Even a small creature can prove capable of a great kindness
Lions should never sleep in open lairs
Hunters are always able to outwit the animals they trap
Mice are more dangerous to lions than they appear

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the Lion about to do to the Mouse right after he catches it?
options: Question it
Release it at once
Carry it outside the lair
Kill it

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Mouse say as it begs to be let go?
options: "I was only passing through"
"Please let me go"
"Take me to the hunters instead"
"I will fetch you some food"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Mouse say to the Lion once it has freed him?
options: "I hope you have learned your lesson"
"Do not thank me, thank the hunters"
"Even a Mouse can help a Lion"
"Now we are even, and nothing more"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Lion's decision to release the Mouse make possible later on?
options: The Mouse is free to come to his rescue when he is trapped
The Mouse warns other animals to avoid the Lion's lair
The Mouse leads hunters away from the Lion's territory
The Mouse teaches the Lion how to avoid nets

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Mouse remind the Lion that he once laughed at its promise?
options: To ask the Lion to laugh again
To warn the Lion not to trust hunters
To apologize for waking the Lion earlier
To point out that the Lion misjudged what the Mouse could do

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Mouse acted "without more ado"?
options: It waited quietly before doing anything
It got straight to work without delay
It asked the Lion for instructions first
It hesitated out of fear

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Lion traps a Mouse to test its courage
A Mouse tricks a Lion into freeing it from a net
A Lion spares a Mouse, and the Mouse later returns the favor
A Lion and a Mouse compete to escape from hunters
